section_summary: This section completes one and contains eight additional weekly despatches summarizing Japanese newspaper opinion from late March through May 1949. The principal themes are economic stabilization, balanced budgets, taxation, reparations, labor disputes, Socialist Party divisions, the Chinese Civil War, and emerging Cold War arrangements such as the North Atlantic Pact and the Berlin blockade. The despatches also record debate over Japanese neutrality, women's status, constitutional democracy, prisoner repatriation, participation in international conferences, and the reopening of the stock exchange.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending March 24, 1949 (Despatch No. 176, conclusion)
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan; signed by Cloyce K. Huston for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Concludes a survey of Japanese editorials on the conflict between Democratic Liberal Party campaign promises and occupation-directed economic stabilization.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo newspapers generally concluded that the Democratic Liberal Party could not fulfill its campaign pledges while implementing General Headquarters' balanced-budget proposals. Several papers emphasized that compliance could bring substantial United States aid, while Yomiuri argued that the party should still fulfill as many promises as possible and should have anticipated the nine-point stabilization directive before the election.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending March 31, 1949 (Despatch No. 195)
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan; signed by Cloyce K. Huston for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese editorial opinion on Chinese peace negotiations and Japan's stabilization budget and taxation.
subfiles.summary: Japanese editorials were deeply pessimistic about peace between China's Nationalists and Communists, especially after the Communists appeared to abandon “new democracy” for a more orthodox communist line. On domestic policy, newspapers accepted the priority of the nine-point stabilization program over Democratic Liberal campaign promises but questioned whether projected tax revenues could actually be collected. Tokyo Times argued that deflation, business failures, and unemployment might be unavoidable stages in restoring economic health.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending April 7, 1949 (Despatch No. 211)
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan; signed by Cloyce K. Huston for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese editorials on the North Atlantic Pact, the national budget, and Premier Yoshida's policy speech.
subfiles.summary: Newspapers generally treated the North Atlantic Pact as defensive and potentially conducive to peace, while also urging both the Soviet Union and Western powers to overcome mutual suspicion. Commentary on Japan's budget accepted the necessity of following General Headquarters' stabilization proposals despite their severity. Editorialists sharply criticized Premier Yoshida's policy speech as meager, derivative, and lacking concrete measures, with Akahata attacking him especially harshly.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending April 14, 1949 (Despatch No. 230)
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan; signed by Cloyce K. Huston for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Reports press discussion of the Socialist Party convention, Japanese neutrality, and the status of women.
subfiles.summary: Editorialists saw the Socialist Party's fourth convention as a test of whether its incompatible left and right factions could overcome ideological quarrels, factional leadership, and its January election defeat. Asahi criticized Premier Yoshida for questioning permanent neutrality and argued that internationally recognized neutrality remained possible. Women's Week prompted calls for practical gains in education, employment equality, and emancipation rather than ceremonies or abstract slogans.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending April 21, 1949 (Despatch No. 263)
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan; signed by Cloyce K. Huston for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Assesses press disappointment with the Socialist Party convention and discussion of prices, deflation, government payments, and personnel reductions.
subfiles.summary: Most newspapers considered the Socialist Party convention an ambiguous compromise between the Suzuki and Morito plans that failed to overcome factionalism or define whether the party was a class or national party. Akahata denounced the Socialists from the communist left, while other papers urged unity, practical policies, and public education. Economic editorials turned from the balanced budget to industrial subsidies, price controls, deflation risks, delayed government payments, and proposed reductions in government personnel.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending April 28, 1949 (Despatch No. 269)
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan; signed by Cloyce K. Huston for the Acting Political Adviser
subfiles.about: Summarizes reactions to the yen exchange rate, renewed warfare in China, the split in the Japan Farmers Union, and Japanese prisoners in Soviet custody.
subfiles.summary: The new yen exchange rate dominated the week's news, although the despatch concentrated on several additional controversies. Newspapers increasingly expected Communist control of China but warned that governing conquered territory and reconstructing its economy would be difficult. They also analyzed the Socialist-Communist split in the Japan Farmers Union and demanded information and faster repatriation for Japanese prisoners held in the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending May 5, 1949 (Despatch No. 304)
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan; signed by Cloyce K. Huston, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Reviews editorial reactions to negotiations over the Berlin blockade, May Day, and the anniversary of Japan's constitution.
subfiles.summary: Japanese papers welcomed movement toward lifting the Berlin blockade, often attributing the Soviet decision to Western strength following the North Atlantic Pact and plans for a West German government. May Day editorials examined organized labor's democratic development, economic responsibilities, and susceptibility to Communist influence. Constitution Day produced contrasting assessments: Yomiuri called constitutional democracy hollow in practice, while Asahi and other papers defended the constitution's democratic and pacifist principles.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending May 12, 1949 (Despatch No. 311)
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan; signed by Cloyce K. Huston, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Surveys press opinion on Japanese participation in international conferences, the Berlin settlement, a coal strike, and the Shoup tax mission.
subfiles.summary: Newspapers welcomed the United States proposal to relax restrictions on Japanese participation in international conferences, linking international engagement to economic self-sufficiency and eventual access to international finance. Commentators debated whether the lifting of the Berlin blockade would ease tensions in Asia or hasten Japanese and German peace settlements. Editorials criticized the coal miners' strike as a threat to stabilization and urged the Shoup mission to reduce tax inequities, evasion, corruption, and disincentives to work.

subfiles.title: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending May 19, 1949 (Despatch No. 352)
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan; signed by Cloyce K. Huston, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Reports optimistic editorials on suspending reparations, reforming taxation, and reopening Japan's stock exchange.
subfiles.summary: Japanese newspapers welcomed the United States proposal to suspend reparations as a major aid to industrial recovery and economic independence, while warning that capital shortages, raw-material constraints, and structural weaknesses would remain. Tax editorials called for fairer personal and corporate levies, less corruption, lower cultural taxes, and closer attention to local finance and Japanese family arrangements. The reopening of the stock exchange was praised as a return toward economic normalcy and a means of protecting investors and supervising private business.
